reports.title: How does USD appreciation affect commodity prices?
reports.development: A stronger US dollar against major currencies.
mechanism: Most commodities are priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar raises their cost in other currencies and can reduce non-US demand.
Producers outside the US earn dollars but pay local costs, so a strong dollar can lift their margins and supply at a given dollar price.
A strong dollar often coincides with tighter global financial conditions, which weighs on industrial demand and speculative positioning.
countries: Commodity importers with weak currencies (India, Japan, euro area)

precedents.text: The dollar index rose sharply while oil and industrial metals fell; oversupply in oil was also a major cause.
A weaker dollar after March 2020 coincided with a broad commodity rally, alongside stimulus and supply disruptions.

evidence: Dollar index 103.55; 3-month change +3.9%, 1-year +4.0% (Yahoo Finance, 2026-11-17).
250-day correlation of daily dollar-index and gold returns: -0.40 (the expected inverse link holds).
250-day correlation of daily dollar-index and copper returns: -0.34 (the expected inverse link holds).
contradicting: 250-day correlation of daily dollar-index and WTI oil returns: +0.23 (the usual inverse link is not holding).

scenarios.name: Dollar strengthens further
scenarios.text: Historically associated with weaker dollar-priced commodities, unless supply shocks dominate.

scenarios.name: Dollar weakens
scenarios.text: Historically associated with firmer commodity prices and stronger emerging-market demand.

reports.class: AI interpretation (mechanism, precedents, scenarios) with computed evidence (numbers)

reports.title: How do rising US real yields affect gold?
reports.development: A rise in US inflation-adjusted (TIPS) yields.
mechanism: Gold pays no income; higher real yields raise the return given up by holding it.
Higher real yields usually come with a firmer dollar, a second headwind for dollar-priced gold.
Price-insensitive buyers (central banks) can absorb selling by yield-sensitive investors.
countries: Major gold buyers: China, India, Türkiye, Poland

precedents.text: Real yields rose in the 'taper tantrum' and gold fell by roughly 28% over the year.
Real yields rose steeply, yet gold reached record highs in 2024, supported by record central bank purchases.

evidence: US 10y real yield 2.91% (2026-11-13); gold 3,862 with 1-year change -5.2%.
250-session correlation of daily real-yield changes and gold returns: -0.17.
750-session correlation of daily real-yield changes and gold returns: -0.16.
contradicting: Central bank gold buying (321 t in Q3 2026, WGC) has offset part of the real-yield headwind since 2022.

scenarios.name: Real yields keep rising
scenarios.text: Headwind for gold unless official-sector buying accelerates.

scenarios.name: Real yields fall as hikes end
scenarios.text: Removes the main macro headwind identified in the scorecard.

reports.class: AI interpretation (mechanism, precedents, scenarios) with computed evidence (numbers)

reports.title: How does China's industrial production affect copper?
reports.development: A change in China's industrial output.
mechanism: China consumes roughly half of the world's refined copper, mostly for power grids, construction, appliances and vehicles.
Stronger industrial activity raises copper demand and drawdowns from exchange inventories.
Expectations move prices ahead of the data: policy stimulus announcements often lead copper.

precedents.text: China's stimulus-led industrial rebound coincided with copper more than doubling over the year.
China's industrial slowdown coincided with copper falling to multi-year lows.

evidence: Correlation of China's annual industry value-added growth with copper's annual average price change: +0.76 over 9 years (World Bank, Yahoo Finance).
China industry value added grew 4.5% in 2025 (World Bank).
Copper 1-year change +19.4% (2026-11-17).
contradicting: Monthly industrial production and PMIs are not yet connected; annual data hides turning points.

scenarios.name: Chinese stimulus lifts industry
scenarios.text: Historically supportive for copper and copper-exporter currencies.

scenarios.name: Property and industry stay weak
scenarios.text: Copper relies on energy-transition demand outside China.

reports.title: How does Japanese monetary tightening affect global capital flows?
reports.development: The Bank of Japan raises rates or lets long-term yields rise.
mechanism: Japan is the world's largest creditor nation; higher domestic yields make it more attractive for Japanese investors to keep savings at home.
Yen-funded carry trades lose appeal when the funding cost rises and the yen strengthens, forcing position cuts.
Repatriation can lift yields in markets where Japanese investors are large holders (US Treasuries, European bonds).

precedents.text: A BoJ rate rise and a sharp yen rally coincided with a carry-trade unwind; the Nikkei 225 fell 12.4% on 5 August 2024.
Japanese investors are among the largest foreign holders of US Treasuries.

evidence: Bank of Japan policy rate 1.25% (2026-10); 12-month change +0.75 pp (BIS).
Yen against the dollar: 3-month +0.3%, 1-year -2.8% (Yahoo Finance).
Japan FDI net outflows US$172bn in 2022 (World Bank).
contradicting: Bilateral portfolio holdings (IMF CPIS) and Japanese investors' monthly flows (MoF) are not yet connected.

scenarios.name: Faster BoJ tightening
scenarios.text: Risk of yen strength and pressure on carry trades and foreign bonds.

scenarios.name: Gradual normalisation
scenarios.text: Flows adjust slowly with limited market stress.

reports.title: How does European industrial weakness affect German equities?
reports.development: Falling industrial output in Germany and the euro area.
mechanism: Weak industry hurts domestic cyclicals (chemicals, autos, machinery) through lower volumes and margins.
DAX companies earn most of their revenue outside Germany, which dilutes the domestic effect.
Weakness can bring ECB easing and a weaker euro, both of which can support exporters' share prices.

precedents.text: German industrial output fell after the energy-price shock while the DAX reached record highs, led by globally exposed companies.

evidence: DAX 26,341; 1-year change +11.7% (Yahoo Finance, 2026-11-17).
contradicting: German industry value added -1.1% in 2025 (World Bank).
The DAX has risen while German industry contracted: index earnings are global, not domestic.

scenarios.name: Industrial recovery
scenarios.text: Supports domestic cyclicals and mid-caps more than the DAX.

scenarios.name: Prolonged weakness
scenarios.text: Pressure on domestic sectors; ECB easing may cushion the index.

reports.title: How do higher oil prices affect India's trade deficit and inflation?
reports.development: A sustained rise in crude oil prices.
mechanism: India imports most of the crude oil it consumes, so higher prices raise the import bill directly.
A wider trade deficit puts pressure on the rupee, which raises the rupee cost of all imports.
Fuel and transport costs pass through to consumer prices; the government may absorb part through taxes and subsidies.

precedents.text: Higher oil prices widened India's trade deficit and pushed CPI inflation above the RBI's 6% upper tolerance band for most of the year.
Falling oil prices narrowed the deficit and helped bring inflation down.

evidence: Fuel was 33% of India's merchandise imports in 2023 (World Bank).
India's trade balance in goods and services: US$-69bn in 2025 (World Bank).
Energy (HS 27) was 27.78% of India's goods imports in 2025 (UN Comtrade).
Correlation of oil's annual average price change with the annual change in India's trade balance: -0.79 over 9 years.
India CPI inflation 4.2% in 2025 (IMF estimate).

scenarios.name: Oil rises 20%
scenarios.text: Wider deficit, rupee pressure and higher inflation risk.

scenarios.name: Oil falls
scenarios.text: Improves the external balance and gives the RBI room to ease.

reports.title: How does a growing US fiscal deficit affect Treasury issuance and bond yields?
mechanism: The Treasury finances the deficit by issuing more bills, notes and bonds.
More supply needs buyers; if demand does not keep pace, investors demand a higher term premium.
Higher yields raise interest costs, which widens the deficit further.
countries: Large foreign holders: Japan, China, United Kingdom

precedents.text: Heavier issuance after the debt-ceiling deal and Fitch's downgrade of the US (August) coincided with the 10-year yield touching about 5% in October.

evidence: US general government balance -6.5% of GDP in 2025 (IMF estimate).
US gross government debt 122% of GDP in 2025 (IMF estimate).
US 10y Treasury yield 5.12% (2026-11-16).
contradicting: Treasury issuance and auction data (TreasuryDirect, Fiscal Data API) are not yet connected; yields also depend on Fed policy and inflation.

scenarios.name: Recession
scenarios.text: Deficits widen but yields fall as the Fed cuts and investors seek safety.

reports.title: How does foreign investment affect a country's currency and stock market?
reports.development: Large inflows (or outflows) of foreign direct or portfolio investment.
mechanism: Foreign investors must buy the local currency, which supports it while inflows last.
Portfolio inflows raise demand for local equities and bonds directly.
Direct investment is slower and stickier; portfolio flows reverse quickly in risk-off periods.
countries: Emerging markets with current account deficits (India)

precedents.text: A sudden reversal of foreign capital caused currency collapses and equity sell-offs in Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea.
In the taper tantrum, portfolio outflows hit India and Indonesia; their currencies fell sharply.

evidence: FDI net inflows: United States +1.0% of GDP (2025); China +0.4% of GDP (2025); Japan +1.0% of GDP (2025); Germany +1.9% of GDP (2025); France +1.8% of GDP (2025); India +1.0% of GDP (2025); United Kingdom +0.9% of GDP (2025); Canada +3.0% of GDP (2025); Switzerland +0.0% of GDP (2025); Russia +0.4% of GDP (2025) (World Bank).
contradicting: Bilateral investment positions (IMF CDIS/CPIS) and monthly portfolio flows are not yet connected, so flow-to-price links cannot be tested here.

scenarios.name: Risk-on inflows
scenarios.text: Currency and equity support for recipients.

scenarios.name: Sudden stop
scenarios.text: Currency weakness and equity sell-off, most severe where deficits are funded by portfolio flows.
